analysis.one_liner: Requires large warehouse employers to disclose work quotas, provide paid rest breaks, and limit workplace surveillance.
analysis.headline: The bill died without a vote: introduced on September 25, 2024 with 13 Senate sponsors including one Republican, it was referred to the Senate labor committee and never received a hearing or floor vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would set national rules for the country's warehouse and fulfillment workers, the people who pick, pack, and ship online orders. Employers with more than 200 warehouse workers would have to tell every worker, in writing, exactly what production quotas they face, what discipline can follow a miss, and what tracking technology is watching them. It would ban quotas that cut into bathroom use and legally required breaks, guarantee a paid 15-minute break every four hours, let workers see and correct their own speed data, and direct safety regulators to write the first federal ergonomic standard for warehouse work. It never moved.
analysis.who_benefits: Warehouse and fulfillment workers at large distribution centers, including workers hired through temp agencies. They would learn in writing what quotas they face and what surveillance tracks them, gain a guaranteed paid rest break every four hours, be able to request and correct their own work-speed records, bring union or worker-advocate representatives into inspections and complaints, and be shielded from being fired within 90 days of asserting these rights unless the employer can prove a different reason. Workers would also gain the first federal ergonomics standard aimed at the repetitive-strain injuries that warehouse work is known for.

how_it_helps.text: Every covered worker would get a written description of each quota they are subject to, including the disciplinary consequences of missing it, how targets are calculated, and what surveillance technology and third parties are used to collect their work-speed data.

Employers could not impose quotas that interfere with legally required meal and rest breaks, bathroom use including travel time to the bathroom, or legally required accommodations, and could not discipline a worker for failing an undisclosed quota or one based solely on ranking workers against each other.
Workers would receive at least one paid 15-minute rest break for every four hours of work, with anti-retaliation notice and multilingual signs required at the facility.

Workers and their union or worker-advocate representatives could request, at no cost, copies of the worker's own speed data and the aggregate speed data for comparable coworkers, ask the employer to investigate and correct inaccurate records, and have a representative accompany federal inspectors.

Firing or otherwise penalizing a worker within 90 days of the worker exercising these rights would create a legal presumption of retaliation that the employer must overcome with clear and convincing evidence.

Claims under the bill could not be forced into pre-dispute arbitration, unions and worker advocacy groups could file complaints on workers' behalf, and the Federal Trade Commission could enforce the rules as an unfair practice alongside the Labor Department.

The Labor Department would have to issue an ergonomic standard addressing musculoskeletal injury risk and a standard requiring trained first-aid personnel and prompt medical referral for injured workers at covered facilities.

analysis.who_pays: Large warehouse, distribution, e-commerce fulfillment, and express-delivery operators, plus the staffing agencies that supply their workforce. They would bear the cost of documenting every quota, training workers on their rights, providing paid breaks they do not currently owe, limiting and disclosing surveillance data collection, and facing civil penalties of up to $769,870 for willful or repeat violations. Some of that cost would be passed through to shoppers in prices.

drawbacks.text: The bill applies only to employers with more than 200 employees across their covered warehouse-type facilities and only to workers actually subject to a quota, so most smaller warehouses and quota-free workers would get none of these protections.

The bill bars performance targets measured over any period shorter than a day, including targets that rank workers against coworkers or against their own past performance, which reaches beyond abusive practices into productivity-management tools many employers use for legitimate purposes and for productivity-based pay.

Covered employers would carry new documentation, notice, training, and paid-break obligations, and enforcement is stacked across three agencies (Labor, OSHA, and the FTC), which opponents would call an unusual and potentially duplicative compliance burden.

The ergonomics and medical-referral standards would be written by regulation over one to four years after enactment, so the bill's most concrete safety rules would depend entirely on future rulemaking rather than taking effect immediately.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the workers covered, the protections are concrete: knowing your quota, keeping your breaks, seeing the data used against you, and not being fired for asking. The compliance costs fall on an industry with very large employers, not small businesses. The honest weaknesses are scope and design: the bill excludes most warehouses below the 200-employee threshold, its blanket ban on sub-daily measurement goes past obvious abuses, and its strongest safety rules would arrive only through future rulemaking. On balance the bill is designed to help low-wage workers at a real cost to their large employers.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate labor committee the day it was introduced, sat there through the end of the session, and never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Edward Markey introduced the Warehouse Worker Protection Act in the Senate on September 25, 2024, with 12 cosponsors — 10 Democrats, 1 Republican (Josh Hawley), and 1 Independent (Bernie Sanders).
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
The congressional record shows no further action — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action — before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
Because the bill was introduced with barely three months left in the session and was never taken up by its committee, it expired when the Congress ended; bills do not carry over to the next Congress.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large warehouse, fulfillment, and delivery operators came out ahead: they avoided quota-disclosure, paid-break, surveillance, and ergonomics obligations that would have cost them money and constrained how they manage and monitor their workforce. Warehouse workers gained nothing.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's 13 sponsors spanned the ideological spectrum — 11 Democrats, independent Bernie Sanders, and one Republican, Josh Hawley — so the bill never even reached the stage where a party split on it could show up in a vote.

industries.industry: Large warehouse, fulfillment, and express-delivery operators
industries.note: These employers (the NAICS categories in the bill cover warehousing, wholesalers, electronic shopping, and couriers) would have to disclose every quota and surveillance system, guarantee paid breaks, limit data collection to what is strictly necessary for quota monitoring, and face civil penalties up to $769,870 for willful violations. Their existing model of opaque, aggressively monitored productivity quotas is exactly what the bill targets, so their interest ran against the workers the bill protects.

The bill explicitly counts contractors, temp firms, staffing agencies, and leasing entities as covered employers, so agencies placing workers in large warehouses would share the disclosure, break, and anti-retaliation duties rather than escaping them through the contracting structure.

industries.industry: Workplace surveillance and workforce-monitoring technology vendors
industries.note: The bill requires employers to name these vendors to workers, describe what data they collect and where it goes, and restrict collection to what is strictly necessary for quota compliance — shrinking both the market and the opacity these products sell.
